reason: Census of the two fields that sit beside best_used_when on the reward card: all 68 grants and all 68 catch values, read side by side rather than sampled. catch is the strongest writing in the catalog and needs almost nothing -- 'The borrowed verse is the last thing its previous owner ever said', 'The number it gives you is always correct and is never, ever welcome'. grants is where the defects are. (1) 16 of 68 open by naming the reward: 'The Dawnpin locks any hinge', 'Tide Telemetry lets its holder read a hull's stress lines'. The card prints the name directly above, so the subject is spent on what the reader just read -- the identical rule the authoring prompt already enforces for known_for, never applied to grants. (2) Two describe the reward as granting itself: 'It grants a sealed jar' where the reward IS the jar. (3) Four use a gendered pronoun with nobody for it to refer to ('She starts to feel the next breath coming in her own chest'), the pronoun form of the hard-coded-name defect, since a reward card shows the reward alone. (4) One opens on our own taxonomy: 'This skill lets you reprogram edible nanites'. Silas, 2026-09-01, on method: read exhaustively rather than sample, then check the negative space -- all 45 unflagged grants and all 64 unflagged catch values were read and confirmed sound before trusting these checks.

2026-08-11.rewards[item].grants: Not a sentence. 'A single vial of thick green fluid that closes wounds by growing living tissue over them within minutes, visibly rooting and pulsing as it works' is a noun phrase with no main verb -- it punctuates like a sentence and passes every automated check, but it does not parse as one. Rewrite so it has a subject and a finite verb, keeping the vial, the regrowth, and the visible rooting.
2026-08-11.rewards[skill].grants: Not a sentence. 'The ability to read a fighter's injuries and lies at a glance, seeing fractures and fear both laid bare in the same look' is a noun phrase with no main verb. Rewrite as a proper sentence, keeping the injuries-and-lies reading and the single-glance framing.
